title: Henry Ford: When a Business Icon Spread Conspiracies
hero_object: 1920 Original Copy of The Dearborn Independent & 1927 Public Retraction Letter
hook: Henry Ford didn’t just build cars. His newspaper spread antisemitic conspiracy theories.
punchline: Being good at business doesn’t make every claim you publish true.
visual_paradigm: 1920s Industrial Press & Ford Motor Assembly (Industrial Charcoal #18181B, Model-T Black #09090B, Printing Brass #CA8A04)

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Henry Ford didn’t just build cars. His newspaper spread antisemitic conspiracy theories.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Starting in nineteen-twenty, Henry Ford used his wealth to buy a weekly newspaper: The Dearborn Independent. Over ninety-one issues, it published attacks based on the forged Protocols.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Ford required every Ford car dealership to distribute copies to car buyers. Wealth and fame gave an exposed lie a massive corporate distribution channel.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Here’s what happened next. Sued for defamation by Aaron Sapiro in nineteen-twenty-seven, Ford settled, closed the paper, and issued a formal public apology acknowledging the claims were completely untrue.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Yet even today, people quote Ford’s articles without mentioning his own sworn retraction. Success in automotive manufacturing didn’t make him an expert in history.
scenes.on_screen: QUOTE FORD'S CLAIMS? QUOTE HIS APOLOGY TOO.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Authority in one field doesn’t transfer to another. When a billionaire makes a massive historical claim, ask for evidence, not their net worth.
scenes.on_screen: WEALTH & FAME DO NOT VALIDATE CLAIMS

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Being good at business doesn’t make every claim you publish true.
scenes.on_screen: BUSINESS SKILL DOES NOT MAKE CLAIMS TRUE
scenes.source: Beyond the Myth · Facts, not scapegoats
